slides.title: Confirming Understanding, Not Asking New Questions
bullets: Reflective questions show the MSL genuinely understood what the physician said
They invite the physician to confirm, correct or deepen that understanding
Drawn directly from motivational interviewing, an evidence-based communication framework

slides.title: OARS and the Hardest Skill
bullets: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, Summarising
Reflective listening is widely described as the most crucial and most difficult skill in OARS

slides.title: Rephrase the Meaning, Not the Words
bullets: Verbatim repetition can feel mechanical or patronising
Rephrasing captures the underlying meaning behind what was said
Often gently surfaces something the physician implied but did not state
Confirms understanding while inviting elaboration or correction

slides.title: More Insight, Same Conversation Time
bullets: Mostly reflecting, with occasional exploring, beats mostly informing
MSLs typically learn considerably more in the same amount of time
Physicians experience it as more engaging real intellectual work, not passive listening

slides.title: Reflection Slows the Rush to Rebuttal
bullets: Reflective listening naturally slows a conversation down
Reduces the temptation to jump to a data point when a concern is raised
One of the most effective ways to avoid drifting into the persuading mode

slides.title: Practice Through Your Own Call Notes
bullets: Reflective questioning is a skill that improves with deliberate practice
Review call notes for moments where an informing response replaced a reflective one
Look for where reflection would have opened a richer conversation

takeaway.title: Reflective questions keep a conversation two-way without adding new content, and they keep it honest
bullets: Reflecting accurately confirms understanding and invites deeper answers
It surfaces more insight than informing in the same amount of time
It slows the rush to rebuttal, guarding against drift into persuading
